strains.name: Bacillus subtilis
strains.role: Stress tolerance, nutrient uptake, root biofilm and biomass.
strains.finding: Less sodium reached the shoots of plants under salt stress, and chlorophyll ran about 57% higher at the strongest salt level.
strains.source: Han et al. (2014), Frontiers in Plant Science 5:525

strains.name: Bacillus amyloliquefaciens
strains.finding: More of the root growth hormone IAA (auxin) released when tryptophan, an amino acid found in root exudates, was available. Strains that could not make IAA promoted plant growth less.
strains.conditions: Laboratory cultures and plant growth tests.
strains.source: Idris et al. (2007), Molecular Plant-Microbe Interactions 20:619

strains.name: Brevibacillus laterosporus
strains.role: Enzyme activity, nutrient release and root growth.
strains.finding: Fresh weight, dry weight, plant height and lateral root growth all rose significantly, with higher IAA in treated plants as the bacteria colonized the roots.
strains.source: Wang et al. (2022), Horticultural Plant Journal 8:22

strains.name: Bacillus licheniformis
strains.role: Germination, root branching and root-zone competition.
strains.finding: More shoot dry mass, with root mass close to double the untreated plants.
strains.source: Nunes et al. (2022), Brazilian Journal of Microbiology 54:397

strains.name: Glomus intraradices
strains.role: The most aggressive colonizer: phosphorus, water and hard-to-reach nutrients.
strains.finding: Faster phosphate uptake in colonized plants recovering from drought, with root phosphorus about 30% higher.
strains.source: Le Pioufle et al. (2019), Frontiers in Plant Science 10:897

strains.name: Glomus etunicatum
strains.finding: Higher photosynthetic efficiency in colonized seedlings at high salt than in uncolonized seedlings.
strains.source: Incesu et al. (2025), Frontiers in Plant Science 16

strains.name: Glomus aggregatum
strains.role: Trades host carbon for nutrients the root cannot reach.
strains.finding: Uptake of phosphorus, zinc and copper rose significantly, along with dry matter, at every phosphate rate tested.
strains.source: Manjunath, Hue & Habte (1989), Plant and Soil 114:127

strains.name: Glomus mosseae
strains.role: Delivers phosphorus and nitrogen from soil beyond the root.
strains.finding: Of the plant’s total phosphate came through the fungal hyphae from soil the roots could not reach, along with 35% of its nitrogen.
strains.conditions: Couchgrass and white clover, compartment pots.
strains.source: George et al. (1992), Canadian Journal of Botany 70:2130

strains.name: Trichoderma viride
strains.role: Frees bound phosphorus for the plant.
strains.finding: More shoot dry weight when the only added phosphorus was an insoluble organic source, and +34% with insoluble calcium phosphate.

strains.name: Trichoderma harzianum
strains.role: Colonizes and persists in the root zone; root growth.
strains.finding: Rise in Trichoderma populations on treated greens, holding at 100,000 CFU per gram or more through winter.
strains.conditions: Creeping bentgrass greens, four years of field trials.

research.text: Average crop yield gain from microbial biofertilizers in a global meta-analysis, rising to +20% in dry climates, with better nitrogen and phosphorus use efficiency.
research.source: Schütz et al. (2018), Frontiers in Plant Science 8:2204

research.text: Yield increase from mycorrhizal fungi across 13 rainfed crops (546 paired observations), with shoot biomass up 24% and root biomass up 30%.
Average increase in root dry weight from humic substances. Response varies by source and rate; leonardite humics sit at the low end of the range.
research.source: Rose et al. (2014), Advances in Agronomy

research.text: Cation exchange capacity of humus in meq per 100 g, compared with 2 to 15 for kaolinite clay and under 2 for sand. Sandy soils rely on organic matter to hold nutrients.
research.source: Cotching, Brown & Lemon, Cations and CEC fact sheet, GRDC

research.text: Share of feather meal nitrogen that becomes plant-available in 4 weeks (75% by 10 weeks). Poultry litter releases more slowly, about 27% in 4 weeks.
research.source: Sullivan et al. (2019), Oregon State Extension EM 9235

research.text: Increase in mycorrhizal root colonization from reduced tillage and winter cover crops. Practices that protect soil life protect the inoculum.
research.source: Bowles et al. (2017), Journal of Applied Ecology 54:1785
